noticias.titulo: 2434 reproducciones · 76 reacciones | RIO DE JANEIRO — O pastor Márcio Poncio é alvo de buscas da Polícia Federal na Barra da Tijuca, na Zona Sudoeste do Rio de Janeiro. A ação faz parte da nona fase da Operação Unha e Carne, que apura um esquema de lavagem de dinheiro e ocultação de patrimônio de luxo, como aeronaves, carros importados e imóveis de alto padrão registrados em nome de terceiros, mas controlados pela organização criminosa. Ao todo, a PF cumpre quatro mandados de busca e apreensão. Três deles miram salas comerciais ligadas a Márcio Poncio, apontadas pelas investigações como a estrutura operacional e administrativa do grupo. Conhecido como "pastor dos cigarros", Márcio Poncio é empresário, fundador da Igreja da Nuvem e pai da deputada estadual Sarah Poncio. Ele já havia sido preso em julho deste ano, durante a quinta fase da mesma operação. ➡️ #GloboNewsRadar - de segunda a sexta, às 8h30, na #GloboNews. Assista na TV e no @globoplay | GloboNews

noticias.titulo: Murió Fátima Báñez, exministra de Trabajo de España, en el choque de trenes
noticias.resumen: La noticia fue confirmada, entre otras personas, por la presidenta de la Comunidad de Madrid, Isabel Díaz Ayuso; ya son 69 las víctimas fatales
noticias.contenido: El choque de trenes en España se cobró, hasta el momento, 69 víctimas fatales , entre ellas, la exministra de Trabajo Fátima Báñez , quien se encontraba en uno de los vagones del ferrocarril de alta velocidad que impactó en la localidad de Toledo este miércoles. La mujer de 59 años había sido funcionaria del expresidente del gobierno español Mariano Rajoy . La noticia, consignó el diario El País , fue primero confirmada por el portavoz del Partido Popular (PP), Borja Sémper. “Te vamos a echar mucho de menos, querida Fátima, amiga. DEP Fátima Báñez”, escribió en redes sociales, aunque luego borró el mensaje. La presidenta de la Comunidad de Madrid, Isabel Díaz Ayuso , también lamentó la muerte a través de un posteo en redes. “Qué pena tremenda nos causa la muerte de Fátima Báñez en el accidente de tren. Tan buena gente, alegre, dispuesta, solvente… La vamos a echar mucho de menos. España pierde a una gran mujer política", publicó en su cuenta de X . Báñez —que habría cumplido 60 años el próximo 6 de enero— fue la primera mujer en ocupar el cargo en el Ministerio de Empleo y Seguridad Social y fue también la que más tiempo estuvo al frente de la cartera, desde 2011 y hasta 2018 . Entre otras cosas, le tocó gestionar la crisis económica provocada por la Gran Recesión española entre 2008 y 2014. Licenciada en Ciencias Económicas y Empresariales por el Instituto Católico de Administración y Dirección de Empresas (Icade) y con un máster en Gestión Pública de la escuela de negocios IESE, el medio español destacó su rol como una de las colaboradoras más estrechas de Rajoy antes y durante su mandato. Tras haber abandonado la política institucional en 2019, Báñez se dedicaba principalmente al sector corporativo , la consultoría empresarial y la representación institucional de la Fundación CEOE (Confederación Española de Organizaciones Empresariales). El choque en Toledo Báñez era una de las 540 personas que iba a bordo de los dos trenes que chocaron en las inmediaciones de la estación de Urda. Se trata del segundo accidente mortal en menos de un año en la línea que une Madrid con la región de Andalucía . En comunicación con LA NACION , el operador del sistema ferroviario de España, el Administrador de Infraestructuras Ferroviarias (ADIF), indicó que el incidente ocurrido en la mañana de este miércoles se produjo con dos trenes Renfe AVE e Iryo entre Mora y Urda, en la línea de AV Madrid-Sevilla . Producto del choque, que tuvo lugar a unos 150 kilómetros al sur de Madrid, dos vagones de la formación Iryo descarrilaron hacia el terraplén. ADIF es una entidad pública empresarial española, dependiente del Ministerio de Transportes y Movilidad Sostenible, que tiene como objetivo la construcción de líneas de ferrocarril y la gestión de su explotación.​ El tren AVE colisionó contra los últimos vagones de un convoy de Iryo que estaba detenido en la vía . Según le informó una fuente con acceso a la investigación a la agencia Reuters , el Iryo estaba parado cerca ​de ⁠la ⁠ciudad de ​Toledo, por orden ‌del gestor de ​infraestructuras ​ferroviarias ADIF y debido a un fallo en la señalización, antes de ser embestido por la otra formación. Desde las Fuerzas y Cuerpos de Seguridad del Estado en el Punto de Mando Avanzado en Urda informaron que todos los fallecidos del tren AVE iban en el vagón que encabezaba la formación .

noticias.titulo: Choque de trenes en España: los equipos de rescate registran los vagones en busca de sobrevivientes
noticias.resumen: El gobierno de Pedro Sánchez declaró tres días de luto nacional por las víctimas fatales, hasta ahora 69; apuntan a un error humano
noticias.contenido: MADRID (Reuters).- Los equipos de rescate registraban este jueves, desde primera hora, los vagones destrozados , luego de que este miércoles un tres chocara contra otra formación que estaba detenida cerca de una estación en la provincia española de Toledo , con la esperanza de ‌encontrar más supervivientes del segundo accidente ‌mortal ⁠de alta velocidad ocurrido este año en el país , que hasta el momento dejó como saldo 69 personas fallecidas y más de un centenar de heridos. En medio del primero de los tres días de luto que el gobierno del presidente Pedro Sánchez declaró por el violento incidente y en recuerdo de las víctimas, se vio a los servicios de emergencia sacando del lugar de la colisión lo que ​parecía ser un cadáver ⁠envuelto en ⁠una manta. Las grúas, en tanto, trabajaron durante toda la noche para retirar partes de los restos del accidente . Entre los restos, todavía hay un vagón volcado . Con la prudencia lógica del momento, las autoridades confían en que “no haya más fallecidos debajo”. Paralelamente, se están realizando las identificaciones de los cadáveres. A primera hora de esta jornada, confirmaron que había un fallecido más, una persona que estaba internada malherida en un centro de salud local. Se conocieron los dramáticos audios del choque de trenes en España “UME ‌y equipos de salvamento siguen trabajando con mucho cuidado porque todavía ​no podemos afirmar que no quede ningún fallecido” , ​dijo a TVE Esther Padilla, portavoz del gobierno regional de Castilla-La Mancha. “Ayer entró una unidad canina y hoy volverá a entrar. No podemos dar por finalizado el trabajo”, añadió. En medio de este contexto, los maquinistas de España llevaron a cabo una huelga , medida que ya estaba prevista antes de este fatal accidente, para exigir una mayor inversión en seguridad ferroviaria . En tanto, el presidente Sánchez volvió a viajar a Toledo este jueves para participar en una reunión destinada a supervisar y coordinar la respuesta de emergencia. Por su parte, Alberto Núñez Feijóo , líder ‌del Partido Popular, de centroderecha, que actualmente lidera las encuestas de cara a las elecciones anticipadas del 29 de noviembre, tenía previsto desplazarse a la localidad de Urda, cercana al lugar ⁠del accidente. Sánchez reclamó por el “esclarecimiento” de las causas que llevaron a la colisión de los dos trenes. Durante una comparecencia en el lugar del accidente, unos 150 kilómetros al sur de Madrid, el funcionario afirmó que el Estado está volcado en “el conocimiento de cuáles fueron las causas que originaron este terrible accidente ferroviario” . El ministro de ⁠Transportes español, Óscar Puente, dijo este miércoles que el accidente se produjo después ⁠de que varios trenes se detuvieran automáticamente debido a un fallo en las señales . A continuación, aseguró que alguien autorizó a un tren de la empresa estatal Renfe a circular a velocidad normal, a pesar de que había otra formación parada algunos kilómetros delante . Al iniciarse las investigaciones, una jueza de Toledo prohibió el acceso al lugar del accidente a cualquier persona que no participara en labores de emergencia, seguridad, asistencia sanitaria o judiciales, estableciendo una zona de exclusión de dos ‌kilómetros en ambas direcciones a lo largo de la línea ferroviaria de alta velocidad Madrid-Sevilla. El Sindicato Español de Maquinistas Ferroviarios dijo que no quería especular sobre la causa del accidente. “Queremos ‌guardar prudencia hasta conocer con detalle todo lo realmente ​sucedido para no entrar en especulaciones”, declaró el organismo en un comunicado. El mensaje del papa León XIV a España El papa León XIV , a través de un telegrama firmado por el cardenal secretario de Estado, Pietro Parolin, dijo estar “vivamente apenado” tras conocer la “dolorosa noticia” del “trágico” accidente ferroviario ocurrido en la localidad de Urda, Toledo, y ofreció “sufragios por el eterno descanso de los difuntos”. Junto a ello, según consignó el diario El Mundo , el Sumo Pontífice animó a los miembros de los equipos de rescate a “perseverar en los trabajos de socorro y asistencia”. Edición fotográfica: Fernanda Corbani Fotos: AP; AFP y Guardia Civil Española

noticias.titulo: Choque de trenes en España, EN VIVO: qué pasó en Toledo y las últimas noticias del accidente mientras sigue la búsqueda de víctimas
noticias.resumen: El incidente ferroviario se produjo el miércoles por la mañana; el servicio de alta velocidad se encuentra totalmente suspendido; confirmaron una víctima argentina y otra permanece desaparecida
noticias.contenido: El número de fallecidos por el choque de trenes en Toledo subió a 69, informó LA NACION en una nota basada en Reuters . La última víctima murió tras haber sido hospitalizada en estado grave.El balance anterior era de 68 muertos. Los equipos de rescate continúan trabajando y las autoridades no descartan que haya más víctimas entre los restos. Esther Padilla, portavoz de la región de Castilla-La Mancha, detalló en declaraciones a TVE que en el tren AVE de Renfe 2080 iban 397 pasajeros y en el Iryo 6076, 147 viajeros y un bebé. Según pudo constatar LA NACION con el sistema ferroviario de España, ADIF, el incidente se produjo cuando dos vagones de la formación Iryo descarrilaron entre Mora y Urda, en la línea de AV Madrid-Sevilla . El servicio de alta velocidad se encuentra totalmente suspendido hasta nuevo aviso. El accidente ferroviario se produjo este miércoles por la mañana en la estación de Urda, situada en el municipio español de Los Yébenes , en la provincia de Toledo. A raíz del choque, la circulación entre Madrid y Andalucía se encuentra interrumpida debido al gran despliegue de las fuerzas de seguridad y rescate. Dos trenes que circulaban en la misma dirección chocaron en Toledo, España , con un saldo de al menos 68 muertos y 150 heridos. La cifra, confirmada por las autoridades de la región de Castilla-La Mancha , puede aumentar con el correr de las horas ya que viajaban, entre las formaciones, más de 540 personas .

noticias.titulo: ‘Already feeling it’: Northern Amazon waterfall season ends early, hurting livelihoods
noticias.resumen: BOA VISTA, Roraima — “For those who live off the river, water isn’t just scenery: It is also a road, work and income.” That is how tour guide Fredson Guedes, known as “Tarzan,” learned to view the natural world around him over the course of his 55 years. “I work entirely with nature and depend […]
noticias.contenido: BOA VISTA, Roraima — “For those who live off the river, water isn’t just scenery: It is also a road, work and income.” That is how tour guide Fredson Guedes, known as “Tarzan,” learned to view the natural world around him over the course of his 55 years. “I work entirely with nature and depend heavily on it. Just the other day, I was at Serra Grande [an ecotourism destination in the municipality of Cantá, Roraima], working at the Véu de Noiva [bridal veil, in Portuguese] waterfall, but now there is no waterfall anymore. It dried up.” In the Amazonian region of Serra Grande in Brazil, about 50 kilometers (31 miles) from the state capital, Boa Vista, the seasonal waterfall known as Véu de Noiva usually draws visitors from May through early September during Roraima’s rainy season. That changed in 2026. By late July, the water that defines the landscape had already vanished. Fábio Wankler, a geologist and professor at the Federal University of Roraima (UFRR), points to a “super El Niño” as the driver behind the disruption. The phenomenon, unusually intense this year, has triggered a series of shifts in weather patterns that, across various parts of the country, “have caused longer and more intense periods of drought,” he said. The effects are felt daily. The waterfall, whose cascading flows resemble the delicate lace of a wedding gown, sits along one of the primary routes traveled by Guedes, who navigates the Branco River to reach it at least twice…This article was originally published on Mongabay

noticias.titulo: Un ataque ruso con un dron en una estación de trenes en Ucrania deja 14 muertos
noticias.resumen: El hecho ocurrió este jueves en Dnipro mientras continúa una tregua en una ciudad del sur del país bajo ocupación rusa; nueva crítica de Zelensky contra el acuerdo entre Trump y Putin
noticias.contenido: KIEV.– Un dron ruso se estrelló el jueves contra una estación de tren en Dnipro, en el sureste de Ucrania, y mató al menos a 14 personas en un ataque calificado como “espantoso” por el presidente Volodimir Zelensky. Este ataque se produjo mientras Ucrania y Rusia se esfuerzan por mantener una frágil tregua en la sureña ciudad de Oleshky, bajo ocupación rusa desde 2022, donde los residentes llevan meses sufriendo escasez de alimentos, agua y medicamentos. El ataque a la estación de tren de Dnipro impactó en un andén “donde se encontraba un tren de cercanías y un tren de pasajeros de servicio regular”, afirmó Zelensky. A horrific Russian strike on the railway station in Dnipro. The Russians launched a drone attack on a platform where an ordinary commuter train and a scheduled passenger train were standing. Unfortunately, 13 people have been confirmed killed as of now. My condolences to their… pic.twitter.com/2n8TnJnbfW — Volodymyr Zelenskyy / Володимир Зеленський (@ZelenskyyUa) October 29, 2026 “Las sanciones contra Moscú y su maquinaria bélica no deben aflojarse mientras continúe esta guerra rusa”, señaló el mandatario en redes sociales, al lamentar este “ataque espantoso”. Las imágenes difundidas por los servicios de emergencia ucranianos mostraban cadáveres en el andén, rescatistas que ayudaban a las víctimas y dos trenes de pasajeros calcinados con las ventanas destrozadas. Según la policía nacional ucraniana, al menos diez personas resultaron heridas en el ataque. En un mensaje de agradecimiento a las condolencias enviadas por el presidente de Francia, Emmanuel Macron , Zelensky mencionó otros ataques ocurridos en las últimas horas. ”Los rusos atacaron un barrio residencial en Chernihiv con un dron, acabando con la vida de dos chicas. Tenían solo 15 años. En Kremenchuk, un dron ruso tipo Shahed impactó contra un edificio de viviendas; trágicamente, tres personas perdieron la vida ". Thank you, Emmanuel, for your condolences. Unfortunately, the death toll from the Russian strike on a commuter train in Dnipro has already risen to 14. And just a few hours ago, the Russians struck a residential neighborhood in Chernihiv with a drone and killed two girls. They… https://t.co/HedBdYlvVM — Volodymyr Zelenskyy / Володимир Зеленський (@ZelenskyyUa) October 29, 2026 “Se trata de ataques deliberados contra la población civil, de una crueldad descarada, perpetrados por los rusos precisamente mientras se desarrolla la operación humanitaria en Oleshky. Los mensajes de Rusia son claros: quieren que la guerra continúe. Por ello, es fundamental que la comunidad internacional siga esforzándose al máximo para lograr una desescalada significativa, mediante medidas contundentes y una presión adecuada sobre el agresor”, agregó, en un mensaje indirecto para Washington. Desde que inició su invasión a gran escala, a finales de febrero de 2022, Rusia ha utilizado drones para atacar trenes en la exrepública soviética con frecuencia, destruyendo cientos de locomotoras y matando a varios ferroviarios. En septiembre se efectuaron evacuaciones en más de 5800 instalaciones ferroviarias de Ucrania por amenaza de ataque con dron, dijo a la AFP el operador nacional de ese servicio. Las conexiones por tren son esenciales en este extenso país, donde puede tomar un día cruzarlo de este a oeste. Por su parte, el Ministerio ruso de Defensa afirmó que las defensas antiaéreas derribaron 1214 drones ucranianos durante la noche en uno de los mayores ataques con drones lanzados por Kiev. Cerca de la mitad de los drones se dirigían a la capital rusa, indicó el alcalde de Moscú, Sergei Sobyanin. Críticas a Trump La Fuerza Aérea ucraniana informó que había interceptado tres drones a reacción en un ataque diurno, pero que un cuarto logró eludir sus defensas e impactó contra la estación. El director de la compañía ferroviaria, Oleksandr Pertovski, señaló que se había advertido de la amenaza. “Pero desgraciadamente, todavía había mucha gente en el andén ”, precisó en Facebook. Tras el ataque, Zelensky reiteró sus críticas al acuerdo alcanzado este mes entre el presidente estadounidense, Donald Trump, y su homólogo ruso, Vladimir Putin, para que Moscú abastezca de diésel los mercados estadounidense y mundial a cambio de un alivio de las sanciones norteamericanas. “¿Cuántos ataques terroristas de este tipo ha llevado a cabo Rusia contra nuestro pueblo desde que se levantaron las sanciones contra algunos oligarcas rusos y el sector energético, en lugar de reducir la tensión?”, preguntó. Tregua en Oleshky Mientras tanto, el alto al fuego en torno a Oleshky, ocupada por Rusia, se mantiene por tercer día consecutivo. Ambas partes agradecieron a la primera dama de Estados Unidos, Melania Trump, por lo que la Casa Blanca dijo que fue su papel para ayudar a negociar el alto el fuego temporal, de modo que alimentos y suministros médicos puedan llegar a unos desesperados 2000 habitantes atrapados en Oleshky. El papa León XIV también presionó para lograr una tregua. “El alto el fuego ya lleva 54 horas en vigor”, declaró el jueves el defensor del pueblo ucraniano, Dmytro Lubinets, y añadió que las entregas de ayuda debían comenzar al día siguiente. “Las partes están cumpliendo plenamente los acuerdos y no se han reportado violaciones del alto el fuego”. Su homóloga rusa, Yana Lantratova, confirmó que la tregua se mantiene y que ingenieros rusos están trabajando en el desminado de las carreteras de Oleshky. “Ambas partes están cumpliendo plenamente sus compromisos y no se han registrado violaciones”, señaló. “Esto permite que el personal militar continúe despejando las carreteras de minas y prepare un paso seguro para el convoy humanitario”. Los habitantes locales también podrán evacuar, ya sea hacia Rusia o hacia Ucrania, según funcionarios. No estaba claro cómo funcionaría el mecanismo para hacerlo. Lantratova dijo que ella y su equipo iban camino a Oleshky para la entrega de ayuda, mientras que Lubinets llegó a Bielorrusia y se dirigirá a la ciudad desde allí, como parte de una operación que, según Lantratova, llevaba cinco meses preparándose. Moscú y Kiev están interesados en congraciarse con Washington de cara a posibles conversaciones tripartitas el próximo mes entre Rusia, Ucrania y Estados Unidos. Agencias AP y AFP

noticias.contenido: Blanca Yamira tiene 56 años, trabaja como niñera y cobra alrededor de 260 euros por jornada . Un mes bueno factura más de 4.000. Suena extraño, pero es que Yamira no es una babysitter cualquiera. De hecho, lo que hace ni siquiera encaja del todo en esa etiqueta. Ella no se dedica a cuidar niños que se quedan solos en casa. Su función arranca a las nueve de la noche y se prolonga hasta las siete de la mañana, toda una noche durante la que suple a los padres que acaban de tener un bebé. En otras palabras, cuando el recién nacido llora o se desvela es ella quien lo atiende. Mientras, el padre y la madre siguen durmiendo plácidamente en cama. Yamira es lo que se conoce como una ‘night nannie’ . Una persona, dos tareas. La historia (y experiencia) de Yamira la conocemos gracias a Corriere della Sera , que hace poco publicó un reportaje sobre ‘niñeras nocturnas’ que trabajan en diferentes ciudades de Italia. No todas cobran lo mismo ni tienen la misma experiencia, pero por lo general comparten una serie de características: se trata de puericultoras que se desplazan a las viviendas de sus clientes por las noches (habitualmente entre las nueve y las seis o siete de la madrugada) para desempeñar un doble papel. Atienden a los bebés. Y permiten a los padres descansar. En Xataka La lenta pero inexorable "japonización" de España: los nacimientos han caído un 50% desde la época del baby boom Noches en vela . “Siempre estoy ahí, lista para actuar”, bromea Yamira, que ahora mismo trabaja para una familia de Lugano, en Tesino, al sureste de Suiza. Su turno empieza cuando termina el de la mayoría de niñeras diurnas: llega a casa de sus clientes a última hora de la tarde, cambia el pañal del bebé, lo baña y hace guardia el resto de la noche, mientras los padres intentan recuperar las horas de sueño. Si el bebé se despierta, hambriento, es Yamira quien le da el biberón. Solo recurre a la madre si hace falta amamantarlo. “Las niñeras nocturnas no tenemos vida propia. Lo dejamos todo para ofrecer este servicio. Durante años me he despertado cada dos horas por la noche, incluso cuando estoy de vacaciones”, confiesa. A cambio, cobra 260 euros por noche , lo que explica que esté ganando más ahora que cuando trabajaba como empleada de un banco en Ecuador. ¿Es un caso único? Para nada. Corriere della Sera ha entrevistado a otras niñeras nocturnas, como Renata Wetter, de 61 años, que cobra 180 euros por noche. Lo primero que aclara es que ella no es un canguro, ni una simple cuidadora. Al igual que Yamira tiene formación en puericultura, la disciplina que se centra en el crecimiento y desarrollo de los niños. Aunque ambas mujeres trabajan en la misma región, lo cierto es que la figura de las night nannies está extendida y se encuentra en otros países de Europa. Tampoco es exactamente nueva. En 2018 el diario británico de The Guardian ya hablaba de ellas a raíz del estreno de Tully , una película en la que Charlize Theron interpreta a una madre abrumada que acaba recurriendo a los servicios de una niñera nocturna. Por entonces (2018) ya era relativamente fácil encontrar night nannies en Reino Unido, donde a finales de los 90 se fundó una agencia especializada en ese servicio. Su promotora fue una madre incapaz de encontrar niñeras especializadas en cuidados nocturnos. Menos de una década después gestionaba una red con 200 cuidadoras repartidas por Inglaterra que habían atendido a más de 10.000 familias. Y eso que su tarifa no era barata: 155 libras esterlinas. Bastien Jaillot (Unsplash). En el radar de las empresas . El gran atractivo de Yamira o Wetter es que no solo son puericultoras que se encargan de cuidar bebés. Eso lo pueden hacer también las niñeras convencionales. Ellas se encargan de velar por el descanso de los niños… y de sus padres, a los que evitan noches en vela, entre pañales y biberones. Esa promesa es lo suficientemente interesante como para que ya haya empresas que financian las niñeras nocturnas a sus empleados. Lo contaba hace unos años Financial Times citando el caso concreto de una startup londinense que llegó a una conclusión interesante: las nights nannies quizás no sean baratas, pero facilitan que los empleados que acaban de tener un bebé lleguen a la oficina descansados y, por ende, rindan más. La empresa mantiene las bajas por maternidad remuneradas, pero ofrece un servicio de “niñera nocturna” como extra. Un negocio que crece . Lo cierto es que el cuidado de los recién nacidos y (sobre todo) de sus padres está alentando un negocio en alza. Lo vimos hace poco en China, con los “hoteles de lujo” para madres. Y puede verse también en Europa, donde ya operan expertos que ayudan a las familias con bebés con problemas para conciliar el sueño. No es tan extraño si tenemos en cuenta que el descanso es un activo codiciado: se calcula que un estadounidense promedio pagaría 290 dólares por una noche de descanso “perfecto”. En Xataka Los padres pierden materia gris en las primeras seis semanas de paternidad, y es una buena noticia “Un regalo para la familia” . ¿Quién recurre a las niñeras nocturnas? ¿Se trata de un servicio al alcance solo de familias acomodadas? Aunque las tarifas de Yamira no están probablemente al alcance de todos los bolsillos, Corriere della Sera sugiere que las nights nannies están más extendidas de lo que pueda parecer. Eso sí, no todas las familias las contratan para largos períodos. Algunas se conforman con tenerlas durante los primeros días del bebé. El diario italiano comparte por ejemplo el caso de una abogada milanesa de 38 años que ha contratado dos niñeras antes incluso de dar a luz. La idea: que la ayuden durante la primera semana, cuando más necesitará descansar. “Con nuestro primer hijo, mi pareja me regaló un anillo precioso. Esta vez le pedí que nos hiciera un regalo para toda la familia: contratar a una puericultora. Ya se lo he dejado claro: ‘No quiere anularme como persona ni verme obligada a despertarme ni una sola vez en toda la noche”, confiesa . A pesar de los reparos de su madre, la mujer de 38 años reconoce no sentir “culpa alguna” por descargar parte de la crianza de su hijo en una niñera nocturna. “Para mí es una cuestión de salud mental, un entorno positivo beneficia al bebé”. En Xataka Llevamos décadas mandando a las embarazadas a la cama por precaución. La ciencia acaba de demostrar que es un gran error Un cambio más profundo . El fenómeno de las night nannies es interesante porque conecta con algo mucho mayor: un cambio en la maternidad y la configuración de los hogares. Desde hace tiempo las estadísticas muestran que la maternidad se está retrasando en Europa y cada vez más mujeres dan el paso de convertirse en madres pasados los 35 años . Eso implica también que es más frecuente encontrarse con primerizas que tienen ya carreras profesionales asentadas y un buen nivel de ingresos que les permite acceder a nuevos servicios. También es más común que se hayan mudado por motivos laborales, con lo que viven lejos de sus padres. No es un fenómeno exclusivo de España ni Europa. Algo similar ocurre en China , donde está floreciendo un próspero negocio que se dedica precisamente al cuidado de mujeres durante el puerperio, las semanas posteriores a dar la luz. Hay incluso centros de lujo que ofrecen estancias de lujo por más de 10.000 euros al mes... o incluso por encima de 50.000. Imágenes | Frankie (Unsplash) y Bastien Jaillot (Unsplash) En Xataka | Las tendencias sobre maternidad llevan años impulsando un perfeccionismo extremo. Ahora hay una rebelión: las "Madres Beta" - La noticia "Es una cuestión de salud mental": cada vez más padres están pagando hasta 260 euros la noche a niñeras nocturnas fue publicada originalmente en Xataka por Carlos Prego .

noticias.titulo: “Desconecte, vuelva a conectar y reanude marcha normal”: los audios entre ADIF y los trenes del accidente en España
noticias.resumen: La primera hipótesis apunta a un “error humano”; los muertos ya son 69; las autoridades siguen buscando entre los escombros
noticias.contenido: En las últimas horas salieron a la luz los audios de los maquinistas involucrados en el choque de trenes ocurrido este miércoles en Toledo, España, y un operador del centro de control de Atocha antes de que sucediera el impacto que dejó al menos 69 personas fallecidas. “Desconecte, vuelva a conectar y reanude marcha normal” es una de las frases que investigan los especialistas para intentar determinar qué ocurrió. La primera comunicación se dio entre el conductor del AVE, la formación que impactó contra los últimos vagones del Iryo y un controlador . Si bien el audio que se difundió públicamente se corta por momentos, se escuchan órdenes claras luego de que se registrara una falla en el sistema LZB, utilizado para trenes de alta velocidad. Se conocieron los dramáticos audios del choque de trenes en España “Fallo de transmisión por bloqueo”, le avisan al conductor . Luego de una serie de consultas, el trabajador de la torre de control le pidió al maquinista que reanudara la marcha. “Desconecte y vuelva a conectar el LZB”, manifestó el controlador. “Reanude marcha. Con marcha normal”, agregó . “Vale, de acuerdo”, respondió el maquinista. La orden de retomar el camino y realizarlo a “marcha normal” es la que se marca como un error debido a que no se revisó a cuántos kilómetros se hallaba el próximo tren, en este caso el Iryo . Esa formación estaba a 25 kilómetros y para una marcha normal está establecida una distancia mínima de 30 kilómetros . El reglamento señala que en estos casos debe realizarse una marcha “a vista”, con un límite de velocidad de 40 kilómetros por hora. Por otro lado, la maquinista del Iryo se contactó con la central por el mismo problema, tras caerse el sistema LZB. “No me está permitiendo el tren reiniciar el sistema LZB y por eso estoy detenida” , señaló. “Cuando pueda, dale, y si tiene un problema, nos llama”, le contestaron desde la torre de control. “He tenido una pérdida de transmisión. No he cogido transmisión”, informó minutos después la conductora. “¿Se encuentra detenida ante la señal de entrada?“, le preguntaron . Luego de la respuesta, la orden fue la misma que al Iryo. Desconectar y volver a conectar el sistema LZB y reanudar la marcha . “Perfecto, muchas gracias”, cerró el contacto la maquinista. Pero el tren no alcanzó a arrancar. Fue impactado sin aviso previo por el AVE . Diecisiete minutos, entre las 8.36 y las 8.53 hora local, le llevaron al AVE a impactar desde atrás al Iryo. Las primeras hipótesis apuntan a un “error humano de un operador de Administrador de Infraestructuras Ferroviarias española (ADIF) ante una avería del sistema principal de señalización” , según los medios locales y las propias autoridades del gobierno de España.

noticias.titulo: Ghostly Cat’s Head Nebula lurks within sight of Hubble and Webb
noticias.resumen: The NASA/ESA Hubble and the NASA/ESA/CSA James Webb Space Telescopes recently stared at an eerie star-forming scene within the Carina Nebula, a massive gas and dust cloud located approximately 7500 light-years away from Earth. The two telescopes offer complementary views of the shadowy form, nicknamed the Cat’s Head Nebula, which reflects the 'magical'' process of star formation. Hubble’s visible-light view shows the cat as a dark, elongated dust pillar and hints of young forming stars, while Webb’s infrared-light imagery unveils many stars and other hidden details.

noticias.titulo: Anthropic is asking Wall Street to believe in AGI
noticias.resumen: Today on Decoder, I’m joined by Joey Brookhart, an analyst at the chip and AI research firm SemiAnalysis, to help me dig into the story inside the numbers of the Anthropic IPO filing — a document known as an S-1. Anthropic just filed its S-1 to go public on the Nasdaq, and it could start […]
noticias.contenido: Today on Decoder , I’m joined by Joey Brookhart, an analyst at the chip and AI research firm SemiAnalysis, to help me dig into the story inside the numbers of the Anthropic IPO filing — a document known as an S-1. Anthropic just filed its S-1 to go public on the Nasdaq, and it could start trading as soon as next month at a valuation of anywhere between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion. That would immediately make it one of the most valuable companies on the planet. But the price tag really isn’t the whole story here. The S-1 document published earlier this week is hundreds upon hundreds of pages filled with details that finally paint a picture of the economics of a frontier AI lab. As you might imagine, that picture is both really complicated and built on a series of very, very ambitious assumptions about the future and what AI will do to it . So I wanted to have Joey on the show to help break down what this document tells us, both about Anthropic’s finances and the broader AI economy. Joey and his colleagues at SemiAnalysis actually built a model of Anthropic’s finances from the outside back in July, so he’s been waiting for this filing about as eagerly as anyone, and I was excited to hear his take on what we’ve learned and, importantly, what we still don’t know. Okay: SemiAnalysis’ Joey Brookhart on the Anthropic S-1 and the costs and risks of building frontier AI. Here we go. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Joey Brookhart, you are an analyst at SemiAnalysis. You’re also co-lead on SemiAnalysis’ Tokenomics model, which is going to come up a lot in this episode. Welcome to Decoder . Yeah, thanks so much, Nilay. I am very excited to talk to you. We’re talking just a couple days after the big Anthropic S-1 was filed. It’s our first look inside of the finances of one of the leading frontier models. What’s your take? What’s your read into it? It was an awesome S-1. It’s been a rough three weeks since the investor day. Some people were somewhat disappointed in the September [annualized recurring revenue] numbers, but what we saw here was a company that has efficiently scaled to an amazing level, with a $1 trillion-plus valuation, $70 billion-plus of ARR in a very short amount of time. In gross margins, compute margins, and free cash flow, everything is what you’d want to see. So I don’t think there was much to nitpick in this filing. It’s the reason you’ve seen a lot of the semiconductor complex, and the neoclouds and compute stocks, really rally again in the last two days. It’s funny, I don’t think I can nitpick the S-1 itself. I want to get into some of the details because there are a lot of numbers in there that are worth thinking about. I actually just want to start at the really big picture. You run a thing called Tokenomics. I’m going to explain what Tokenomics is to people. I look at Anthropic and where it could go. I look at Dario Amodei saying that he can see his way to $1 trillion in revenue. Where does that money come from? Because so much of these businesses are about eating every other business and it feels like someone else has to make some money to pay Anthropic to generate these revenues. I haven’t actually seen that laid out very clearly. Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here . Not a subscriber? You can sign up here . It’s so interesting. Today, because even the scale we’re at is $120 billion of ARR between the two leading labs, it’s still an extremely narrow market. The top 1 percent of customers are the ones that are spending $50,000 to $100,000 per employee. Your broader Fortune 500 or Global 2000, which typically do a lot of IT spend, isn’t spending much. A lot of the spending, especially at Anthropic, is coding-specific. It’s almost a single vertical company. We look in the future to 2027, you think to this broader adoption and white collar work. This typical enterprise Q4 budgeting season, we actually haven’t gone through with one of these labs yet in any meaningful way because their ARR did really start to accelerate until the beginning of the year. We think of other cases like cyber, which can be similar to coding, where these are eight-figure-plus contracts with leading enterprises that can scale very quickly due to all the cybersecurity incidents we’re seeing. You get to other verticals like bio. To get to $1 trillion, we do have to move to some of that white collar work, where it goes from AI augmentation to labor saving or replacement in some areas. You look at things like Microsoft’s buyout offers to employees as an example of this , but there’s no wealth of other verticals that they can get into and really start to move the needle. This is the single biggest question I have, not just about the S-1, but the entire industry. I would understand that if there are one or two leading labs. There are two big companies that have a technology that can automate a whole bunch of things. We will see how well that automation goes sector by sector, but there are not just two leading labs. There are quite a few of them. There are open weight models. I’ve heard from a lot of CEOs who are very nervous about giving all their data to an OpenAI or Anthropic and they would like to run some things on-prem. There are law firms running on-prem AI now, which is the funniest turn in maybe all of history. How do you see that playing out? Because so much of the pressure on this S-1 was the numbers themselves, which I want to talk about, but then there’s the external pressure of, “You’ve got to grow and growth is not as short.” So how do you see all of that playing out? It’s very interesting because when we look at coding today, for example — and I think we saw this in Q3 with OpenAI kind of catching up — there are areas of coding where there are very low switching costs, and I can just move between that. What we hear from enterprises and maybe, too, on the OpenAI side — obviously I think they somewhat botched the Fable release, and the lack of zero data retention is why we saw some of the slowdown. That’s something they can fix with Fable 5.5 and maybe drive more enterprise adoption there. That’s a huge thing for enterprises when we talk with them. We definitely see enterprises now, and more so, too, a lot of the AI natives, doing custom training and post-training on open weight models, and then running either their inference off of that or even their products for internal or external use cases. Obviously, DeepMind at Google and [Meta Superintelligence Labs] are very well-funded labs that have pretty similar training compute capacity, and they’re bringing on a ton of it. Not even to mention SpaceX as well, with what Elon said on [about] 10 net new gigawatts next year and half of that is the long-term internal use case. In the first half of the year, Anthropic ran away with it. They were 90 percent of the industry’s net new ARR. We saw in Q3 that OpenAI was probably actually the majority of industry net new ARR. Open-source has grown from probably $1 billion of token inference costs, ARR, in Q1 to $10 billion-plus here in Q3. So yes, the industry’s gotten much more competitive, but there are all these new use cases, too, and some of these verticalized use cases are really where we’re going to see the growth going forward. Because it’s obvious coding isn’t going to power us to even triple from here. It’s interesting. The concept is called Tokenomics. You run that practice alongside another co-lead at SemiAnalysis. Explain what it is because to me it’s such a smart way of thinking about, “We’re going to put some money in and maybe we’ll get some money out.” I think of it as the unit economics [of AI], or even just the broader idea — everything from a macro- to microeconomics of running an AI business or even looking at AI demand. So we cover the hyperscalers, now some of the neoclouds as well in a separate product. But then just the AI labs, too. For investors, or just people that are interested in the business, Anthropic had negative 94 percent gross margins on inference two years ago. Now they have a positive 85 percent margin, and people don’t understand how they allocate compute. How do we think about the inference business model? Part of that gross margin conversation is the revenue per megawatt in inference. Why are all companies that are running inference seeing massive gains in inference and compute efficiency? So we try to model out these businesses and obviously when Anthropic was private, we’re dealing with information we can get from the press and things like that. But now that we have concrete audited numbers, it’s easy to explain the unit economics of this. And also how the businesses differ. OpenAI is a much different business than Anthropic just in both their consumption versus subscription and then historical weight versus consumer versus enterprise. [We are] trying to understand across the demand level the economics of these businesses. Several years ago when I talked to Google CEO Sundar Pichai about the cost of inference, I said, “How are you ever going to make money?” He was just very clear. He said, “If there’s one thing Google’s good at, it’s bringing this stuff down the cost curve.” It was a very blunt answer. I understand how Google can do it. They make their own chips. Anthropic is running on everyone else’s clouds. The core part of the S-1 is how much they’ve committed to spend on other people’s clouds: SpaceXAI, Google, Amazon. Where does their efficiency come from? There’s really token throughput. They have a very diverse chip fleet. Between Trainiums, TPUs, and GPUs, across all of those, we see a ton of token efficiencies. Token throughput, for example, on Trainium chips is up 5x to 10x year-over-year right now. Dealing with both the hardware level efficiencies and the software — and how the model interacts with the hardware — there are a lot of token throughput gains where if you’re doing X tokens per second, now you’re doing five or 10 times that just a year later. What they’ll tell you is they see continued compute efficiencies as well going forward. Max Kan, who co-leads Tokenomics model with me at SemiAnalysis, and I have even published some research on this. Right now, if Anthropic’s at $65 million of revenue per inference megawatt, this was mid-teens last year at this time. What we’ve said on maybe Opus 5.5 on a [Nvidia] Blackwell, you can get to $100 to $120 million of revenue per megawatt. The big thing here is they’re paying on average now just a little over $10 million per megawatt in [cost of goods sold], or just in compute costs. What you can do with those margins is then reinvest in training. People don’t realize this, but only about 30 percent of the compute is actually in inference-serving revenue. The rest is for experimentation and research, training models, and post-training models. So there’s a lot of compute that is building the next model and that’s more of the R&D side and where you actually get your returns and defensibility in this business. Actually, what I was expecting to see in the S-1 was that dynamic play out much more strongly — that Anthropic makes a bunch of money selling the models they have now and there are more customers in the future for the models they have now. That’s going to throw off a whole bunch of margin. And then, because it is Anthropic and they think they’re building a digital god, they’re going to train the next models as much as they can. That is a very particular Anthropic story. The company is chasing AGI. The people who work there will happily tell you that in the S-1 that Claude might be conscious and this could all go to hell. Anthropic is a very unique company in its conception of itself. But you don’t really see that dynamic playing out in the S-1. They’re managing their training costs against their inference margin pretty well. Do you see that going up or changing in any way? I agree. Long term, and we’ve even said this internally, they want to actually increase the percentage of training. If you believe you’re building a digital god or going towards AGI, and as long as you have the gross margins of 85 percent-plus on inference to do so, you can. They’ve grown a lot faster than they thought, and they didn’t expect to be at 11 percent non-gap EBITA margins. They’d love to be closer to zero, or even below that if they could get that compute and allocate it towards training and continue to see these compute efficiencies. They’ve messaged that, too, to investors in the roadshow. You can look at this S-1 and just the curve of profitability over the last few years and how little cash they burned to get to this point and you can say, “This is a good business model, but we’re going towards AGI. Don’t expect the margin leverage we’re seeing to continue to this level, even though long-term margins can be quite a bit higher.” There are some real shades of Amazon there. Jeff Bezos famously told investors he wasn’t going to make money until he could make a lot of money. Obviously, Amazon and Anthropic have a lot of back and forth. Maybe there’s some family resemblance there. But I’m curious, there’s a point of model capability that would allow you to go into more verticals than just coding, right? We might be at it now. The idea of capability overhang exists, the idea that the models we have today could go and take over bio research. They’re taking over mathematics today. There’s a point at which the smartest business decision is to stop training and to just sell your profitable model into more and more companies. Anthropic as a public company will face that pressure. Do you think they’re organized or structured to fend it off? Yeah, I think they’re structured well. With some of the voting stock in areas like that, they definitely are. We’ve seen this in tech before and even publicly when Mark Zuckerberg has made these decisions before to invest heavily. It didn’t always pay off. I just want to point out, it didn’t always pay off. Yeah, it did not always pay off. Although you and I technically are in the metaverse right now, by some definition. [Laughs] Right. But I think that’s something, and there’s an interesting number in the S-1 that 80 percent of revenue in the last three months comes from models released in the last six months. So then you say, “Okay, 20 percent of the models are like Opus 4.5 in earlier versions.” One thing going forward is that if you’re a frontier model company, you always need to be at the frontier and it’s incredibly competitive. Wait, can I ask a really dumb question about that? Yeah. Why? I think the heart of my curiosity about the industry right now is if you enabled some bleeding-edge technology that could revolutionize the entire world, at some point, the most profitable thing to do is to just go play it out in all the different verticals, right? It’s not to go make the next one. It’s actually to run an efficient model in legal services and medicine and wherever else that there hasn’t been diffusion of AI yet. This idea that you always have to be at the frontier, that Anthropic always has to be competing with Google and OpenAI and whoever else, I get it from their self-conception. But from a business point of view, an AI-enabled business is going to throw out more money and spend more money with me, the AI provider, and that isn’t necessarily related to being at the frontier. There are a few portions of that. For new verticals, and this is very cyber specific, if an adversary is using a frontier model, you need to be defending with a frontier model. Fair enough. When we talk to some enterprises, it’s not like an email summary where I can run that on open source or Sonnet. There are just certain verticals where having… [For example,] if you were in a legal case as a defendant, would you be okay if your lawyer was using a non-frontier model if the prosecution— [Laughs] I got bad news for you about what’s going on in the legal market right now. The competitive dynamics do dictate that. I think from a go-forward perspective, we’ve seen this with open source too catching up in one point, but the demand will be there. [SemiAnalysis CEO] Dylan [Patel] says this a lot. The demand will always be there for frontier intelligence, especially in competitive industries. And there are certain tasks, as you go towards more labor replacement versus labor augmentation, where that also is the case. At the same time, they are getting more vertical. If you go look at job postings or what they’re hiring for, they’re putting out more of these SKUs and areas, and there’s a lot of beta testing going on like Claude for financial services, Claude for legal, their cyber program. They’re giving away 25,000 of credits per month for people in their cyber program. That’ll be a huge SKU for them in 2027. Those verticalized areas and then ones that are specifically where you need to be… It’s more adversarial, I should say, or competitive, are the main reasons why. But we can both agree there are areas like email summary and work that definitely doesn’t need to happen [at the frontier]. I’ll just make a dumb comparison to the iPhone. It’s iPhone season. I just reviewed the iPhone Duo. Apple kept the iPhone looking the same for several years now. They build all of the tooling for the new iPhone and then they just reuse it for two or three or four models to get all the value out of that investment back before they move on to the next thing. Apple puts out a new iPhone, and it keeps selling the old iPhone for a while to get more value out of that investment and that development program. The AI industry does not seem to be doing that. All of their emphasis is on developing the next new thing, deprecating the old thing pretty fast, and moving you onto the new expensive product, while at the same time they’re building the next new expensive product. At some point it feels like that will rationalize, that there will be something that is worth just collecting margin from while they go invest in the new thing. I just can’t figure out where Anthropic sits in that cycle. I mean, we do see this. Open source token volumes are picking up and there’s a lot of areas, yes, where the open source models have become good enough. I think on a go-forward basis, you’re like, “Okay, was that because of distillation?” And then the frontier labs have some defensibility actually going forward. I think when we talk to clients, it’s also about how we actually think about frontier versus open source. So something like a Sonnet type model, if you want to do the iPhone 18 versus the SE type analogy. We do see that dynamic, and obviously with open source, it’s a question of how much that can take. Two, because we’re so early in these verticals, we don’t know what’s going to be fully agentic. There’s no human in the loop where the harness actually has, I should say, some value and defensibility to it. The big area I’d look at here, especially when we talk to enterprises today, is only the coders are allowed to use the frontier models at a lot of these enterprises. If you’re a non-coder, some of these companies just limit you to Sonnet, if you’re an Anthropic customer. That’s reflective of how management views and wants to budget for this, what frontier intelligence is actually worth to them in certain areas. In my financial analyst brain, Claude could not build a good financial model six months ago. It’s getting better if you connect it to the right areas, but we’ve gone from something like, “I needed a junior analyst six months ago,” to, “Maybe I don’t as much anymore,” and then, “Will I have a full junior analyst at my disposal anytime or multiple pretty quickly, if I have unlimited token budget?” We just look at that across every vertical and major job category. The time horizon in each of those categories is going to be different. That’s just one of the bigger questions I have: How quickly do they get to where they think they can go? I want to dig in on some of the numbers here. The one that jumped out in all of the comment sections on all of the forums and all of our articles yesterday was $80 billion. Anthropic lost $80 billion [in the first half of 2026]. That is related to a technical charge. Can you just explain the $80 billion? Because it doesn’t seem particularly relevant to the revenue and profits they’re talking about. Yeah, it’s a non-cash charge because their valuation has gone up so much and they’ve issued warrants or convertible notes. You have to account for that in your balance sheet. It’s just a non-cash charge because their valuation has gone up so much since they issued these warrants and notes. That’s something you would always back out. You can argue on stuff like stock-based compensation. Should we really be thinking about that on a non-GAAP cash basis? Because it’s non-cash, if I just hand employees shares, I have to account for that on my income statement, but I’m not actually handing them pure cash out of my bank balance. So it’s not an area like that. It gets the accounting, the high level. If you don’t know accounting, it looks bad, but it’s because they’ve grown so much and their valuation has gone up so much. Some of the argument here about that charge is that Amazon was the other party there. Obviously Amazon’s very happy because Anthropic is buying a ton of AWS and sure they’re happy the valuation has gone up, but over time Amazon’s going to get diluted this way. That’s part of the dynamic there. Anthropic is going to obviously IPO. They’re going to put a bunch of shares in the market. It’s very clear that over time they will issue more shares to raise more money. It doesn’t seem like they’re going to stop wanting to raise money anytime soon. How are you thinking about that in terms of just investment into a company like Anthropic, that your valuation might be going up, but your actual ownership stake might be getting diluted over time? The deals have always been very creatively structured. The number is they’ve actually only burned $10 billion of cash. They have $120 billion-plus of cash and marketable securities in the balance sheet today, and post-IPO, probably another $100 billion. It’s a great deal for both parties. They only really rent compute. It’s not like they have these massive capital outlays or even rent-to-own. You can make some arguments about certain accounting and there are these massive compute commitment obligations and that’s technically future debt, or that is sitting somewhat off balance sheet essentially. But from a dilution perspective, all tech companies dilute. Are they going to need to raise another $100 billion of debt or equity at some point? Possibly. Can they continue to creatively structure and finance future compute buildouts? Probably as well. I know there’s been a lot of angst about the future of compute financing and data center financing in the last few weeks. But if you’re Anthropic, if you’re a major lab, a hyperscaler or Broadcom or Nvidia that are backstopping a lot of these deals, that’s probably not going to change anytime soon. So I’m not particularly worried. As an equity investor, would I be worried about getting super diluted? I don’t think so. If you believe in this long-term AGI bull case and that Anthropic is going to be a leader in this, that probably shouldn’t worry you. You’re probably looking at a $10 trillion-plus business. They can outrun dilution at that point. Let’s talk about the compute commitments. I saw at least one analysis saying over the next 10 years, it’s $800 billion-plus in commitments to the various hyperscalers and neoclouds. That’s a lot. You’re saying that they don’t have that much money. They haven’t even spent that much money yet. Do you see them generating the revenues to pay off those commitments? Yeah. I think when people look at the headline commitments, the $500 to $600 billion number over 7 to 10 years, let’s call it, what they’re paying for compute today actually isn’t that many gigawatts. If you think about their spending right now, on average they’re close to $11 million per megawatt in spend, or $11 billion per gigawatt. If you take that back to the annual level and say, “Okay, the $520 billion number is over 70 years, for example, that’s really not that many gigawatts and they’re going to be well beyond…” When they get to something like 20 gigawatts, the future compute commitments that they’re running essentially is going to be well into the trillions. So yes, they are going to have the revenue to do so. It’s more about how much revenue they are going to have relative to how much compute. Two, the compute efficiency equation. If they keep getting a lot more revenue out of every inference megawatt, how much do you really want to invest in training and take margins to zero from a rental perspective? Because you can get to something where even 80 percent to 85 percent of their fleet is just on training and research at these kinds of margins. The revenue is going to scale pretty well. They’re not in any dire situations there. Unless we realize all this revenue disappears or people churn. It’s not like they have to hit a trillion dollars of revenue extremely, extremely quickly to achieve all this and pay for this. Unless you’re trying to build digital God and unless it doesn’t diffuse across the economy as fast as everyone wants it to. Those are bets, right? They’re huge bets. The numbers you look at, if you’re really bullish on this ramp into the digital economy, is Anthropic saying within their Fortune 500 customers, they have 50 percent of the Fortune 500 and that is just 0.1 percent of their total customers’ operating expenses. When you look at that on a per user basis, it’s like $8 a month if you believe OpEx doesn’t include the cost of goods sold. If you believe they include the cost of goods sold, it’s sub-$50 per month. They said the same thing. Of the top 5 percent of Claude Code users, they’re spending $18,000 a year on average, the top 5 percent of users. Their non-Claude Code users spend under $75 a month, well under $75. There’s this huge opportunity, especially when we talk to enterprises and these traditional buyers of IT software. Penetration is extremely low in traditional white collar work. That’s the big point, too, that there is a large ramp period here of both seats adoption and usage. You can make arguments of who’s going to win in this, but it’s obvious the frontier labs are going to get some portion of this and it’s going to be pretty material to net new ARR next year. One of the things that’s really interesting about that is we talk about the frontier labs, we talk about the hyperscalers — Anthropic has a lot of wild risk factors in this S-1, including that Claude might be conscious and kill us all. But one of the most direct and maybe easiest to understand is that AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud are both suppliers and competitors in some real way, particularly Google. And they say, “These relationships could turn.” They have a big relationship with SpaceXAI. Elon Musk is going to train Grok. They’re going to compete with SpaceXAI at some point. That relationship might become precarious. As you say, they’re only renting their compute. At some point, the market might force them to own more of their compute because their own competitors don’t want to lease their capacity to the leading company. How do you see that playing out? We definitely see both OpenAI and Anthropic going more direct and not owning the compute, but more rent-to-own, or going through an SPV as some financial sponsors do and producing the compute more directly versus renting. There are two points to this. Google, from one perspective, is also selling its external chips to customers and saying, “We don’t care to monetize this within Google Cloud or even allocate the share… If you think we’re very chip-constrained, we don’t even care that these are going to DeepMind or internal GCP compute for us to monetize. We’re just willing to become a chip seller.” Anthropic loves TPUs and there are 3.5 to 4 gigawatts-plus, and probably more in the pipeline, in terms of orders there of Anthropic buying these chips directly to then rent. So yes, the market is good. Wait, it’s not buying them directly to rent. So they’re buying them into a neocloud? Yeah, they buy them through an SPV, or the SPV buys them and then they rent it from the SPV. Got it. Okay. Even within Google Cloud or AWS or Foundry, Anthropic is massive — 48 percent of their business comes through the Bedrock Foundry and Vertex where people are paying through their existing cloud relationship to access these models. They’re not even talking to Anthropic. You don’t have to interact with the Anthropic sales force. You mentioned this earlier. This marketing channel where Anthropic gets a rev share. Right. If you’re AWS and you’re saying, “I’m running Anthropic compute for, let’s say, $10 million per megawatt, but now I’m getting 16 percent of $65 billion-a-megawatt plus the compute costs as well,” so we’re seeing margins at all the clouds go up right now. Part of it is CPU utilization is going up because of all the coding and then some on the [reinforcement learning] side, but these token-as-a-service businesses as we call them — so AWS Bedrock, Microsoft Foundry, Google Gemini Agent Enterprise platform, which is formerly Vertex — are actually massively increasing the margins on AI at these clouds. They’re benefiting as well when shareholders are giving them credit for this recently. In Q2, both Azure and AWS had extremely, extremely strong quarters, AWS specifically, on the back of Anthropic’s growth on Bedrock. Do you think that will keep Amazon from ever wanting to train its own frontier models? They’re doing a good job of letting AWS be the infrastructure for everybody else, but they’re one of the only big tech companies that hasn’t felt the insecurity of not having their own models. Yeah, it’s interesting. Amazon is very happy to serve a wide variety of customers and they have very little [frontier capability]. When we look at our estimates of training compute, they have the least of any hyperscaler, except maybe Oracle. It doesn’t seem like there’s much strategy there. I know Microsoft in the last two quarters has been talking about it a little more. AWS on the call has been talking about it a little more, but it’s not huge. They’re not doing it to the same extent that Meta is or trying to be competitive here or even Google with Gemini. Especially someone like Dylan will tell you, if you’re not trying to compete at the frontier, there’s really not a place for you, especially if you’re only dedicating a few hundred megawatts internally. One, internal use case is like serving Amazon retail, but then two, training. There are a lot of commitments to make to be good at this. It’s a conversation for a different day, but I look at these Microsoft job cuts and I see it as the glimmer of evidence that they’re going to try to compete in the future. They obviously got burned pretty badly by OpenAI. Yeah. They have, in the new agreement that they signed, the right to monetize OpenAI models for essentially not paying OpenAI anything within that agreement. They’re going to have some interesting things ahead where they monetize the OpenAI models or even through Microsoft 365 Cowork and Copilot applications where they’re not paying OpenAI anything for a frontier model. The other dynamic here, and you brought it up earlier, is over the last few weeks, there’s just been a lot of stress about neoclouds — whether they will succeed, whether they will fail. I think Elon Musk said there will be a guppy-like extinction event , which is just a brutal metaphor to use to describe a bunch of data centers. But this is a bunch of circular financing and Nvidia stood a bunch of them up and maybe the hyperscalers are just going to run away with it. Maybe Anthropic’s demand, because maybe they will want to own more of their own compute because renting it is precarious in all these ways. What do you make of the neoclouds? Do you think they’re going to survive the market actually shaking itself out as these companies go public? Elon obviously has some incentive to say neoclouds are going to be extinct. ClusterMAX said something else and just does amazing ratings of the neoclouds . There are a lot of neoclouds that are ex-crypto miners that are not good businesses and are not good at operating clusters. I just want to point out CoreWeave is an ex-crypto mining company, right? Yeah. I don’t mean CoreWeave, but there are others further down the list. CoreWeave, Nebius, and anyone that has backing or backstops from one of the major labs, hyperscalers, Nvidia, or Broadcom is going to be okay. It’s that longer tail. Hyperscalers have been 65 percent of CapEx and net new compute brought online. There’s 35 percent of the market that doesn’t have the balance sheets that the hyperscalers have. Both Google and Meta have recently raised or announced they’re going to raise. When we look at the big four hyperscalers, they don’t actually need to raise that money over the next two years, even though CapEx is growing from $1.2 to $2 trillion pretty quickly. But for a lot of these other neoclouds, if you don’t have that sort of backing, I think it is very hard, even right now, and becoming extremely difficult if you don’t have the backing or backstops from those players to keep building compute. It’s a very, very tough financing market. One of the things I think is really interesting about Elon in particular talking about neoclouds dying and obviously hyping up his own data center business is he’s trying to put them in space and to get away from the backlash in the United States around data centers in particular. We have a lot of coverage about data center backlash in the United States, it is slowing down a lot of projects. But at the rate we’re going, if you think the neoclouds are shaky, you might actually end up abandoning a bunch of GPUs and half-built data centers or have them tied up in financing agreements where they can’t be lit up. What do you make of that? Do you think we actually just need to go to space? Or do you think the market is going to rationalize and actually take advantage of all the compute that is currently allocated but not being used? We’ll rationalize more so. The market is very good at finding places to put chips here on the ground. Politically, we’ll see what happens next week with midterms and the fallout from that. Obviously, there are some very large sites that still have massive permitting problems. There’s the entire power equation as we look towards next year. The data centers will be built. There will be a method to get these built. The biggest thing — and the hyperscale CFOs have said this — from an overbuilt perspective and on a relative basis, it’s pretty cheap to build the data center shell. What they can do if they overbuild is they’re going to say, “We’re just not going to take delivery of the chip. We’re not going to buy chips. We’re not going to fill them up.” They’ll just sit empty and chipless. But the majority of the spend is on the chip side. So if we do end up in a place where we’re actually oversupplied from a data center perspective, I know that’s a little bit different. It’s the exact opposite of what the question was. They have said that from an ROI perspective. This comes back to that larger question of whether we are still going to be super supply constrained. A lot of people now, especially in the last three weeks, are talking about, “Are we in this massive glut of compute as we look towards 2028 actually?” Because the same thing we talked about from Anthropic going from negative 94 percent margins to positive 85 percent and compute efficiencies mean as you bring on more inference megawatts that are making a lot more revenue per megawatt, all else SQL, you need less compute. So it’s a question of whether we we going to have enough revenue in 2028 to justify the ROI on $2 trillion plus of CapEx. This is why I spent so much time asking about capability overhang and how good the models are today, because you can see some competitor that is less idealistic about AGI saying, “Actually, we’re going to do a bunch of forward-deployed engineers in all of these verticals where they haven’t taken advantage of AI and sell them high-margin inference because we’ll automate big chunks of their business and they’ll see the return.” Right now, a bunch of the Fortune 500 has not seen a return on AI spending . So if you’re actually just better at customer service and deployment and productizing the model, you might get way ahead of where Anthropic needs to be because they’re still thinking about AGI every single minute of every single day. I look at Dario standing next to Marc Benioff at Dreamforce and that dude does not want to be there right now. He wants to be thinking about the machine god. There’s something there where you can just see competitors coming up with an open source model and saying, “We’re actually going to productize this and we will actually take the revenue that everyone else is depending on.” Yeah, it’s extremely, extremely interesting. In the interim, that’s why it is getting more verticalized because you need something to bridge AGI where it just fully does the job, you need something to bridge the actual model today. [Laughs] Yeah. We’ll just take that for granted. To get there, you need some bridges of where it sits with the actual end user at some point. Everything is going to come down to this: Is there going to be some timing or adoption mismatch where we just don’t get the revenue at a certain point of time to justify that chase of “train and compute towards AGI”? That’s a risk. The other risk we look at is whether we get more models at the frontier even at the open source that are as competitive in coding, where token pricing across the frontier needs to be taken down, because like I mentioned earlier, there are lower switching costs. Even at SemiAnalysis, we went from 95 percent or 90 percent-plus of our usage at the end of Q2 was on Anthropic’s models down to 70 percent after the release of OpenAI’s ChatGPT 5.6 and Astra. And then with Opus 5.5, it’s gone back to 90 percent-plus roughly. It does come back. Even the base of revenue today — and they’ve said that we have net revenue retention of 900 percent, so they’re seeing this massive, massive growth. This isn’t a traditional software business like ServiceNow or Workday, where you have just an incredible logo or gross retention of 95 percent to 98 percent and customers sign these nice three-year contracts, they never churn, they add some seats, and maybe they adopt another product that is being upsold. This is purely consumption. The other portion was the 20 percent drop in the last two weeks of the year versus the prior two weeks last year in token spend, because of the holiday season. You’re not going to do work code stuff, you’re not going to be coding for work during the holidays. This is extremely, extremely pure consumption business, even different from how we think about Snowflake or Datadog today in public markets. Obviously, Anthropic is not the only company that’s going to have an IPO. OpenAI is right next to them. They’ve delayed theirs. You mentioned earlier Anthropic is much more enterprise focused. I think OpenAI for a long time thought that Google wouldn’t react to them and they would just take the search business away and everything would be fine. Google obviously reacted for better or worse. Search is now AI Overviews. Looking at the Anthropic S-1, what are you looking ahead to with OpenAI? Because they are a more consumer facing company. OpenAI was 60-40 consumer, 60 percent consumer and 40 percent enterprise at the end of Q1. That didn’t flip for the first time until January or August to be enterprise focused. What they’ll tell you is enterprise business — because it was so consumer and subscription focused, this consumption business that’s 80 percent of Anthropic’s revenue — didn’t take off until a release of 5.6 and then with Astra. Those are really great models. OpenAI took the majority of actual net new ARR in Q3, but it’s going to take some time because what’s been in the Wall Street Journal , like negative 100 percent EBITA margins versus we’re seeing positive 11 percent here. There are some differences, some pretty big differences, in the business model where they just don’t monetize at the same rate that Anthropic does. That’s a little bit because the business makeup — the verticals, that consumer-versus-enterprise split — and that’s changing. What they’ll tell you is they see a really good Q4 and they have a much stronger enterprise sales function than Anthropic has. I expect them to come up, but I don’t think the financials are going to look as good as this even when they drop their S-1 maybe in early 2027. Do you think that’s why they delayed it? To get their financials looking better? Yeah, I think OpenAI had a really strong Q3 . Enterprise grew 100 percent quarter-over-quarter versus the total business which was 77 percent. You get another strong quarter of enterprise here. If Opus 5.5 didn’t take a ton of share, that would put OpenAI in a much better position to tell the story. There are some other turns here between now and when Anthropic actually goes public. They’re going to do a roadshow. There’ll be some pricing events. What are you looking for from Anthropic? They did an investor day two or three weeks ago where they did give some more color. I think they’ll walk through why Q3 was so weak. Meta was a very, very large customer, probably over 10 percent. What’s been publicly reported is they went from 60,000 Claude Code seats down to 30,000. These token volumes didn’t disappear, they just shifted into Meta’s internal models. Anthropic started cracking down on anti-distillation, and that was 5 percent of revenue prior. I think they said 5 percent to 7 percent of revenue in the S-1 and stuff against their terms of service. So what’s here on the roadshows is a lot of this October acceleration after Opus 5.5. We believe that they’re back on track. If they were doing $10 billion of net new ARR per month in Q2 and that fell down to $4 billion in Q3, that they’re getting back on that $8 billion to $10 billion pace here in Q4. People want to hear about these new verticals, specifically cyber. They’re doing some patching until they have that full cyber SKU rolled out, but they’re definitely monetizing cyber today for vulnerability code scanning. These are not small contracts, I should say, with existing customers. I think they’ll start to message what the 2027 ARR growth path looks like. The other thing too is expectations management, keeping numbers low enough, not talking about AGI as much. [Laughs] It’s hard to do expectation management when your risk factors are like, “We could pose an existential risk to all of humanity.” [Laughs] Right. And so saying you do that — you’re going to achieve AGI at some point, you’re going to replace everyone’s jobs — but then trying to keep numbers low enough for Q4 and to have this massive beat the first quarter you become public and have a decent guide for 2027, it’ll be a nice mix of seesawing between that long-term vision and short-term expectations management. There’s a lot going on. Joey, this has been great. We’re going to have to have you back as these companies barrel towards actually being public and their economics become much more visible. Thank you so much for being on Decoder . Thank you so much. I appreciate it. Questions or comments? Hit us up at decoder@theverge.com. We really do read every email!

noticias.titulo: Qué pasó con Flavio Bolsonaro y su huida a Estados Unidos: el recorrido, su paso por la Argentina y las últimas noticias hoy
noticias.resumen: El gobierno de Milei negó haber participado en la huida del excandidato presidencial, amparado por la administración Trump; la Bolsa de San Paulo cayó 2,7% tras confirmarse que el excandidato brasileño aterrizó en Miami
noticias.contenido: BRASILIA.- En la repentina salida del excandidato presidencial Flavio Bolsonaro de Brasil rumbo a Estados Unidos, menos de tres días después de su derrota electoral frente a Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva , hay una figura central que impulsó al senador a huir del país y que ideó una serie de estrategias para poder hacerlo posible: su hermano, Eduardo Bolsonaro . Según pudo saber el medio brasileño O Globo , Eduardo Bolsonaro fue el principal artífice de la huida de su hermano. Él y el expresentador de Jovem Pan, Paulo Figueiredo, habían mantenido conversaciones con autoridades del gobierno de Donald Trump sobre la necesidad de acoger a Flavio en caso de una derrota. Eduardo viajó a Florida con su esposa y sus hijos para recibir a su hermano y por la noche posteó una foto del reencuentro. “Foto de hoy, después de reencontrarme con mi hermano, Flavio. Fue un día largo, quizás el más largo de mi vida. Pero prevalecimos. Incluso desde afuera no renunciaremos a Brasil”, publicó. Apenas siete minutos después de que el Tribunal Superior Electoral (STF) confirmara la victoria de Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva (PT) en el balotaje de Brasil, la Policía Federal pidió al juez Alexandre de Moraes que incautara el pasaporte de Flavio Bolsonaro, que había arrancado como favorito en las encuestas y terminó con una sorpresiva derrota. Esa misma noche de domingo, el magistrado, enfrentado con el bolsonarismo y a cargo de una causa por lavado de dinero que involucra al senador del Partido Liberal (PL), aceptó el pedido. La orden se ejecutó el lunes por la mañana, cuando el excandidato salía de visitar a su padre, Jair Bolsonaro, bajo arresto domiciliario por intento de golpe de Estado. En un video publicado por la tarde, el senador descartó cualquier posibilidad de abandonar Brasil, una idea que había alimentado su hermano Eduardo, radicado en Estados Unidos, en caso de una caída en las urnas. “Nunca pensé en salir del país. Voy a entregar mis pasaportes y defenderme de esta aberración, que es un claro intento de intimidarme”, afirmó. Esa fue la última vez que se lo vio en suelo brasileño antes de emprender la huida. La publicación de Flavio Bolsonaro En medio del asombro mundial por la huida de Flávio Bolsonaro de Brasil después de perder el balotaje, este domingo, contra Luis Inácio Lula da Silva , fuentes del gobierno de Javier Milei negaron a LA NACION haber colaborado en la maniobra de escape del excandidato. Desde la Casa Rosada insistieron, además, con que no tienen constancia de que Bolsonaro haya ingresado al país antes de volar hacia Estados Unidos, como deslizan algunas versiones este martes. “No tenemos nada que ver” , refirieron fuentes oficiales ante la consulta de LA NACION . Esto, luego de que el diario Folha de Sao Paulo informara que la administración de Donald Trump habría participado en el plan para sacar a Bolsonaro junto a su esposa Fernanda y a sus dos hijas de Brasil, y que podría otorgarle asilo político. Un avión Gulfstream G400 de la empresa de vuelos privados Baires Fly estuvo retenido por 24 horas en el Aeropuerto Internacional Cataratas del Iguazú hasta que el excandidato presidencial brasilero Flavio Bolsonaro logró despegar junto a su familia rumbo a Guayaquil , Ecuador, en medio de la prohibición dictada por la Justicia por las causas en su contra.
